newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, Gazprom discuss gas supplies after cuts.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, Gazprom discuss gas supplies after cuts.

text.p: Russian gas monopoly Gazprom head Rem Vakhirev held closed talks with Ukraine's leadership on Wednesday after the company reduced supplies to its neighbour over unpaid debts.
Meanwhile, a top aide to President Leonid Kuchma called for "demonopolisation" of the former Soviet republic's wildly inefficient energy market.
"The meeting had more of a political than economic nature," Dmytro Markov, a presidential spokesman, said of the 45-minute talks between Leonid Kuchma and Vyakhirev in Kiev.

"They discussed basic things but not minor ones. They didn't discuss payments and things like that but talked about principal mechanisms and schemes for supplying gas. They had no basic disagreements."

A frustrated Gazprom, fed up with countries not paying for the gas they consume, cut flows on Tuesday to Ukraine by about one third and to Belarus by 50 percent. Supplies to Ukraine were down to around 37 million cubic metres (mcm) per day. Deliveries to Belarus resumed on Wednesday.
Interfax-Ukraine news agency said on Wednesday that Ukrgazprom had cut all gas supplies to Ukraine's Crimean peninsula, which is mostly populated by the ethnic Russians.
Ukraine, the world's single largest consumer and conveyor of Russian gas, is due this year to import 53 bcm of Russian gas. It will transport about 125 bcm through its territory to Europe.
Ukraine owes Gazprom $3.5 billion for 1992-94 supplies, including $1.4 billion already restructured for 12 years with the first $221.5 million tranche to be paid by the end of 1997.
Ukraine has allowed private traders to import and distribute Russian gas since 1995. But the system has not improved the bad payments record of previous years.
Ukraine's two leading private traders, Energy Systems of Ukraine (UESU) and the Intergaz company, owe Gazprom $150 million.
Former Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, who resigned earlier this month, was the architect and main defender of the private traders' scheme.

Critics said the scheme was monopolistic and linked Lazarenko to UESU, to which the government gave the lion's share of gas distribution contracts to supply Ukraine's two most powerful industrial regions, Dnipropetrovsk and Donetsk.

"The state of the gas market needs serious involvement in terms of demonopolisation and artificial transfer of foreign debts into domestic ones," Anatoly Halchynsky, Kuchma's top economic advisor, told a news briefing on Wednesday.

"This state of affairs should be corrected. We are losing a lot transferring all debts onto our population and enterprises," he added, referring to a 6.7 billion hryvnias ($3.6 billion) backlog in unpaid wages, pensions and student grants.
Some analysts suggested it was unlikely Ukraine would return to the state-owned Ukrgazprom monopoly, which handled all gas imports and distribution in the past.
But they said quotas might be redistributed to traders who would also be asked to provide more cash payments.
"Gazprom was forced to pay all debts to the Russian state budget and it now desperately needs cash," Alla Yeremenko, an energy commentator at the Zerkalo Nedeli weekly, said.
"Gazprom is not happy that most payments from Ukraine are in goods and not in cash."
Yeremenko said so far only up to five per cent of payments were made in cash while the rest was settled in goods ranging from pipes and metals to soap and food.
"The Russians want at least half the payments made in cash," he said.
